texts.period: Legend romance adapted and translated by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 1, eBook #78208

summary.en: In the olden time when Hpyeng-Yang was the capital, the high dignitary Sun-Yen, beloved as a disinterested protector of the people, finds three of the King's subjects dead of starvation by the roadside while a grand banquet is being given. He goes straight to the King and reproaches him: 'Who pays the expenses of your amusements? Your people and no one else.' The King summons the Prime Minister Ja-Jo-Mi, the Unscrupulous, who has secretly conceived the scheme of usurping the throne, and Sun-Yen's frankness marks him out. The Prime Minister writes a letter full of bitter criticisms and threats against the King, signs it with Sun-Yen's name, and drops it in the path of a police agent in the darkness of the Korean night. 'Where there is smoke there is fire,' says the King; Sun-Yen is banished to the island of Kang-Sin and the scholar San-Houni, compromised in the plot, to Ko-Kum-To.
summary.zh: 平壤高官順緣，見餓殍三人於道，即入宮諫王曰：『王之宴樂，皆出於民；民飢而王不恤。』王召宰相子兆迷——其人陰懷篡位之心。子兆迷乃偽作逆書，署順緣之名，夜棄於巡捕之道。王曰『無風不起浪』，遂流順緣於江心島，其友山湖泥亦坐累徙於古金島。

sensitivity.note: Adapted Korean legend romance; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: While on his way Sun-Yen's attention was suddenly drawn to a great crowd of people by the roadside. His servant learned the reason: they were about to carry away several people who had died by the highway. 'Sire,' he said to the King, 'several of your subjects have just died of starvation by the roadside... Who pays the expenses of your amusements? Your people and no one else, and the Governors instead of doing their duty are also leading a frivolous and even vicious life.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 1 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: This official, Ja-Jo-Mi, was a man whose severity of character and conduct had earned for him a terrible reputation; no one knew of it, but he had conceived the scheme of usurping the throne. Feared that he might be removed by the revelations of Sun-Yen, he resolved to find a pretext for his exile: he wrote a letter full of bitter criticisms and threats against the King, signed it with the name of Sun-Yen, and, adopting a disguise, dropped the missive in the path of an agent of police in the darkness of the Korean night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 1 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Sire, it often happens that we are deceived by those whom we deem most faithful. As far as Sun is concerned, I consider him perfectly capable of this infamous business.' 'That's enough, my faithful Ja-Jo-Mi. Have Sun thrown into prison. He will be tried immediately.' The King withdrew, leaving Sun in despair, and ordered the Prime Minister to banish Sun at once to Kang-Sin; San-Houni, who was also compromised in the plot, was exiled to Ko-Kum-To.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 1 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: Cheng-Si Sells Herself for Three Hundred Bags of Rice

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 2, eBook #78208

summary.en: Exiled to Kang-Sin, Sun-Yen's wife dreams of an angel from Heaven bending over her, and bears a daughter, Cheng-Si — but dies three days after the birth. From shedding so many tears Sun becomes blind, and his thirteenth-year daughter keeps him from starving by begging. When he falls into a pond, the disciple of an anchorite saves him and predicts: within three years you shall recover your sight and become Prime Minister — but he must be paid three hundred bags of rice. Cheng-Si hears of the merchants' ancient practice of purchasing a young girl in each village to throw into the sea, forestalling the perils of the Yellow Sea crossing. She offers herself for the rice, hands the debt-paper back to her father telling him she sold only her liberty, and then, at parting, confesses the truth: 'It was not my liberty but my life which I gave in exchange for the three hundred sacks of rice. I have to plunge to the bottom of the Yellow Sea to pray for a favorable passage for our sailors.' With another hundred bags given for his support and entrusted to the magistrate, she leaves her fainting father — 'Don't worry, we shall meet again in a better place where we shall be happy forever.'
summary.zh: 順緣妻夢天使而生貞施，三日後卒。順緣淚盡而盲。貞施行乞養父。某夜翁墮池，為苦行僧之弟子所救。弟子曰：『三年之內，爾目當復明，且為宰相；惟須施米三百石以代禱。』女聞海商歲以處女投海以祈安航之古俗，乃自請以身易米。父知之，慟絕。女以百石託於邑宰，含淚別父曰：『勿憂，他日吾儕當於極樂之地重逢。』

sensitivity.note: Human-sacrifice motif summarized; parallel to Sim Chung (cf. korean-simchung-indangsu-leap).

passages.text: Now it came to pass one night that Sun's wife had a dream: she saw an angel from Heaven bending over her. The truth was that this noble lady was soon to become a mother, and it was not long before she gave birth to a daughter to whom they gave the name of Cheng-Si; but scarcely three days had passed when her mother died. From having shed so many tears, Sun became blind. His greatest regret was in not being able to look upon the face of his little daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Happily Sun-Yen's cries were heard by the disciple of an anchorite who lived in a cave on the mountain slope. 'I predict, indeed I can read in your face, that your evil days will not last forever. Within three years you shall recover your sight and you shall become Prime Minister... you must pray diligently to Chen-Houang, the Emperor of Heaven. You must give me three hundred bags of rice and I will pray in your stead... It will be sufficient if you bind yourself in writing to pay me when you have the means to do so.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the days of our story, Korean merchants in search of business were accustomed to make one trip a year across the Yellow Sea. Thinking to avoid the danger, the merchants had recourse to a very ancient and very barbarous practice: in each village where they traded they purchased a young girl, and these victims were thrown into the sea, the perils of the voyage thought to be in this way forestalled. Cheng-Si met one of these traders in search of a human victim: 'You need not look any farther. If you want to take me, I will go, but what will you give me in exchange for my life?' 'Suppose I ask for three hundred bags of rice?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Father, I deceived you the other day. It was not my liberty but my life which I gave in exchange for the three hundred sacks of rice which you promised the disciple. I have to plunge to the bottom of the Yellow Sea to pray for a favorable passage for our sailors.' The blind man fell into a swoon. The merchant, a witness of the scene, said, 'I will give you another hundred bags of rice and we will not set sail for three days.' She sought an audience with the leading magistrate, who consented to take charge of the maintenance of the old gentleman; and 'Good-bye, father, don't worry, we shall meet again in a better place where we shall be happy forever.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 2 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: The Murder on the Open Sea and the Sandals by the Lake

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 3, eBook #78208

summary.en: San-Houni, banished to the desolate rock of Ko-Kum-To, engages two boatmen: the brothers Su-Rung the wicked and Su-Yeng the goodly. On the open sea Su-Rung reveals his designs on the passenger's wife; despite his brother's protests, San-Houni and his servant are put to death before the scholar's wife's eyes, and she plunges into the sea crying, 'In spite of you, I shall die with my husband' — but Su-Rung orders her rescued. The old woman on the beach, herself a ten-year victim of Su-Rung who murdered her husband, helps Yeng-Si escape by night — then, on the road, asks to trade sandals, shows the way to the temple of Buddha, and drowns herself in the lake with Yeng-Si's sandals at the water's edge, that it would appear as if the younger woman had committed suicide. In the bamboo grove Yeng-Si's labor pains come; a nun finds mother and child; the name San-Syeng is traced on the pink flesh of the baby's arm in characters that cannot be removed, inked over, and the mother's ring slipped into the wrappings before the child is laid on a village street corner.
summary.zh: 山湖泥遭流徙，僱舟。舟子兄弟：兄修隆兇殘，弟修永忠厚。至中流，修隆殺主及其僕。山湖泥之妻投海，被救回。登岸後，修隆託老嫗看守。嫗本十年前遭其害之寡婦，夜助新寡脫逃，臨別以己履易其履，指路至佛寺，竟自投湖死，以履留岸，偽為新寡自盡。新寡至竹林而產，僧尼救之。以針刺兒臂曰『山升』，以墨填之，並以己戒指納襁褓，棄於村口。

sensitivity.note: Murder scene summarized; self-sacrifice motif central.

passages.text: As long as they were in sight of the coast, things went well, but when the party was on the open sea, Su-Rung the wicked revealed his designs: 'I am somewhat taken with the wife of our passenger. I want her and I'm going to get her. Her husband grates on my nerves. I must get him out of the way.' 'You are mad,' replied Su-Yeng. 'Do you think for a minute that I will ever allow you to do anything like that?' 'Bah! You are jealous of me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 3 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Su-Rung called the oarsmen: 'Men, I want you to grab that fellow and his servant. Take and keep what money they have on them and kill them. The woman alone must live.' Su-Yeng was forced to obey his brother's injunction; as soon as he had turned his back, San-Houni and his servant were put to death, the murder committed under the very eyes of the scholar's wife. Having no desire to survive her husband, she plunged into the sea, crying, 'In spite of you, I shall die with my husband' — but Su-Rung ordered his sailors to turn about and rescue the unhappy woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 3 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Well, I would consider it a great favor if you would let me have your sandals in exchange for mine... I am very old. You go on. If Su-Rung catches up I will tell him that I do not know in what direction you went... Just a moment. I am going to show you the road which you should take: keep straight ahead until you come to a grove of bamboo, then keep on walking until you come upon the temple of Buddha. When you arrive at this spot, you will be out of danger.' When Yeng-Si had gone a short way, the old woman arose, and taking the sandals, she turned toward a lake; placing them at the water's edge, she uttered a brief prayer and jumped into the water — she did not wish her death to be fruitless, so she placed her friend's sandals on the shore, that it would appear as if she had committed suicide.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 3 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yes, it was a little boy. She seized the poor little being and covered it with tears and kisses. A nun from the temple ran to the spot whence the cries came, and found the mother and child. Since she wished to have some sign which would enable her to recognize her son, Yeng-Si took his arm and with a needle traced on the pink flesh the characters forming the name of San-Syeng, then went over these letters with India ink; finally, slipping off the ring which she wore, she placed it in the wrappings of the child, and started out to place the child at a street corner and then return to the temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 3 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy with the Name Tattooed on His Arm

region.en: Robber's house; roads of Korea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 盜宅與行路（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 4, eBook #78208

summary.en: When the vapors of intoxication have cleared, Su-Rung finds the hut empty; at the lake he sees the sandals and a body floating, and even the murderer is moved — but the brothers find, half an hour later, the baby Yeng-Si left in the village, and Su-Rung carries it home to a nurse, treating it as his own son. The boy grows good to look upon and extremely intelligent; at school his comrades taunt him about having no parents, and one blurts the truth: 'Su-Rung is not your father. He is only a thief and a robber. He found you on a street corner and brought you up.' Accidentally the boy discovers the name San-Syeng tattooed on his arm, and finds a ring while rummaging among old books and papers. At seventeen he asks leave to travel through Korea; overhearing children tell the remarkable story of the robber who found a child abandoned by the roadside, he determines to discover those to whom he owes his birth.
summary.zh: 修隆酒醒，見嫗宅空。至湖，見遺履浮屍。旋於村口拾嬰兒，攜歸養之，視如己出。兒長而慧，同窗譏其無父母，且曰『修隆非爾父，盜也，拾爾於街衢』。兒偶見己臂上刺『山升』二字，又於舊書中得戒指。年十七，辭而行天下，欲尋其親。

passages.text: Instead of retracing their steps at once they continued on their way to the neighboring village and were the first ones to find the baby which Yeng-Si had left there a half hour or so before. Quite pleased at his unusual discovery, Su-Rung took the little being and carried it home with him where he confided it to a nurse, instructing her to take the greatest care of the little boy; the murderer of San-Houni gave all his time to the education of the child he had adopted, treating him as if he were his own son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'No parents,' shouted the indignant boy. 'Why, I have a father, and it is not my fault if I lost my mother before I was able to know her.' 'That shows that you really do not know anything about yourself. Su-Rung is not your father. He is only a thief and a robber. He found you on a street corner and brought you up.' Yeng-Si's son was somewhat reassured by Su-Rung's soothing answer, but other circumstances aroused his suspicions: he accidentally discovered the name of San-Syeng tattooed on his arm, and found a ring one day while rummaging among some old books and papers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: In order more easily to solve the problem of who his parents might be, he determined to travel through the country. When he had reached his seventeenth year, San-Syeng asked Su-Rung for permission to make a trip through Korea in order to finish his education; Su-Rung gave his consent for San-Syeng to travel alone on a journey that would consume perhaps two years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ten O'Clock Moon and the Flight on the Father's Horse

region.en: Garden of the mansion at Yen-Yu (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 4, eBook #78208

summary.en: In the village of Yen-Yu, San-Syeng sees in a walled garden a girl whose eyes rival the stars, and plays on his flute verses of the homeless wanderer who would die and become a butterfly to hover about the adorable flower. The girl, Yeng-So-Yei, answers on her own instrument — the spider spins her web, the swans do not come, but to-day I heard the song of the blue bird — and her dead father appears in a dream ordering her to marry the son of San-Houni stopping at the nearest inn. Meeting by night, she points both hands to the moon: ten o'clock. He fakes a faint; she runs to his help; over the wall passes a letter about the butterfly that throws itself into the flame. Her mother, sleepless, hears the mingled kisses and posts a servant with a sabre to kill the first person who leaves the room; the dead father warns in a dream, and Yeng-So-Yei trades places with the servant, leads out her father's favorite horse, and loads her lover with jewels, silver and her father's favorite sword. 'Take this keepsake,' he says, giving her the ring whose meaning he does not yet guess. 'It is a token of my undying love.'
summary.zh: 山升遊至燕羽，隔牆見一麗人，乃吹笛自詠曰『願為蝶繞花』。女以琴和之，且夢亡父命嫁山湖泥之子。夜會，女舉雙手指月——十時之約也。其母察覺，命僕持刀守門。女夢父警示，以紙易刀，出父之駿馬、寶劍與金珠付郎，郎以戒指贈之。二人灑淚而別。

sensitivity.note: Pre-wedding elopement motif; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: He came to a pause when he saw in the garden a young girl of marvelous beauty: a bright oval face as fresh as a half ripened peach, eyes that rivaled the stars in their brilliancy. One evening, when his sorrow was more acute than ever, he sought distraction in music, stationing himself near the garden and improvising verses: 'Homeless am I — I know neither Heaven nor Earth. I am walking in despair, seeking in vain for those who gave me birth... My most ardent desire would be to die and become a butterfly so that I could hover about this adorable flower.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: The young girl had heard everything. 'If this young man does not know Heaven nor Earth, it means he has lost his parents. If he wants to be transformed into a butterfly to flit around a flower, it means he loves a young girl.' She took her own instrument and in turn improvised: 'The spider spins her web from flower-stem to flower-stem, but the butterfly does not come... To-day, however, I heard the song of the blue bird. He has at last arrived and very soon he will be close and dear to me. The age of sixteen is the fair Springtime of life. If I want to be happy, I should not wait much longer.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it came to pass that her father appeared before her in a dream: 'My daughter, there is stopping at the inn nearest our home a traveler whose merits I bring to your attention. It is the son of San-Houni, the scholar, one of my best friends. I would like you to marry this young man.' The next evening when San-Syeng returned to his post by the garden wall he saw the girl raise both hands and point to the moon. 'The girl raised both of her hands, she must have meant the number ten. Then she pointed to the moon, that surely means at night. She wanted to tell me that she would meet me to-morrow evening at ten o'clock.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her mother, unable to sleep, arose and went walking through the house; passing before the door of her daughter's room she heard above the sound of mingled kisses her daughter speaking with some one. Calling a servant: 'Take a sabre, and place yourself before this door. You are to kill the first person who leaves that room.' But the girl had another dream in which her father warned her, and she traded places with the servant, went direct to the stables, led out the horse her father had mentioned, and turned over to San-Syeng her jewels and silver together with her father's favorite sword. He slipped from his finger the ring which he had found among the books long years before: 'Take this keepsake. It is a token of my undying love.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 4 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: Ja-Jo-Mi Usurps the Throne of the Child King

region.en: Palace and Isle of Cho-To (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王城與鳥島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 5, eBook #78208

summary.en: The King falls suddenly ill, and with the flutter of Death's wings about him commends his young son to the Prime Minister: 'Teach him to govern kindly and finish his education.' The King's death fills Ja-Jo-Mi's soul with joy. When the Governors choose the deceased King's son, the Minister protests furiously that the Prince is too young to rule, condemns the most influential to banishment, and invokes the precepts of the venerable philosopher Kong-Ji: no one can reign in Korea before attaining a certain age. 'You are interpreting the last words of my dear father for your own ends,' replies the young King; 'it is my intention to govern in person.' One bright and beautiful day the King finds himself under arrest and transported to Cho-To, guarded day and night, while the people grumble on every street corner but dare not openly manifest their disapproval. San-Syeng, arriving in the capital, hears the news from his landlord Hong-Jun and resolves to help the unfortunate young ruler — strengthened that night by a dream in which San-Houni appears: 'I was banished from the Capital by Ja-Jo-Mi. While on my way to the island of Ko-Kum-To I was murdered by the robber Su-Rung. Listen: the deceased King's son is in exile at Cho-To. Go, help him.'
summary.zh: 王疾篤，託孤於宰相子兆迷。王崩，子兆迷大悅。群臣立幼主，兆迷怒而逐賢臣，託言聖賢之法：『未及齒者不得臨朝。』幼主曰：『爾借先王遺命以濟私耳，朕必親政。』一日，幼主竟被械送鳥島幽囚。山升聞之，夢亡父曰：『今幼主亦遭其毒，往救之。』

passages.text: The King fell suddenly ill, and sensed the flutter of the wings of Death. 'I am going to die. My great regret is in leaving a son too young efficiently to govern the country... I want my son to succeed me on the throne. Consequently I am requiring of you a further proof of your devotion. Promise me to give this child the guidance of your counsel and wisdom.' Ja-Jo-Mi, the unscrupulous, swore solemnly that he would faithfully observe the last commands of his master; but the King's death filled his soul with joy, for it rendered easier the project he had been dreaming about for so long.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 5 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'You are doubtless well aware that, according to the precepts laid down by the venerable philosopher, Kong-Ji, no one can reign in Korea before attaining a certain age... Your father, my regretted master, on his death bed, requested me to look after the interests of the State.' 'You are interpreting the last words of my dear father for your own ends and in your own interests. He asked you to guide and advise me but did not intimate that you should take my place at the head of the Koreans. Know then, that it is my intention to govern in person.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 5 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the office-holders at the Capital were devoted to Ja-Jo-Mi, for it was through him that they held their places. One bright and beautiful day the King found himself under arrest and transported to Cho-To, the deposed Prince kept under the strictest surveillance all the time. These events had caused a growing unrest throughout the length and breadth of Korea; the people were talking and grumbling, but they did not dare openly to manifest their disapproval.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 5 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: Cheng-Si Rides the Sea Turtle to the King's Prison Garden

region.en: Isle of Cho-To, walled garden (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 6, eBook #78208

summary.en: Dressed for sacrifice, fresh as a new rose, Cheng-Si stands between two immense candles before incense burners heaped with myrrh, consigns her soul to Heaven, and throws herself resolutely into the sea — to find herself resting on the surface: she has struck a gigantic sea turtle, which swims on uncommoded by its burden. Her mother appears borne on the fleecy sheets of a cloud: 'Do not forsake the turtle who has saved your life until he has carried you safely to the shore.' Through a subterranean passage the turtle brings her to a cavern where two polished stone flasks and a letter wait — one drink washes away fatigue, the other clarifies her ideas — and she digs through to find herself in the hollow trunk of an immense tree in an enchanted garden: the residence and place of recreation of the young King exiled by Ja-Jo-Mi. The Prince, who that very day has rigged a rope to a tree bough, forgets his plans of suicide at a single glimpse of a woman; a butterfly leads him to the hollow trunk where he finds her. 'Like you, I am an orphan; I am a son of the late King of Korea.' They marry themselves before an improvised altar — two candles for youth, needle and thread for union — and when a dream of a broken bottle trickling crimson foretells his death, Cheng-Si reinterprets it: the blood signifies the royal purple with which you will be vested. They fire the house and descend through the hollow tree to the sea.
summary.zh: 貞施盛服立於香案，投海。忽有大龜負之而行，母顯聖曰『毋離龜背』。至一洞，得石瓶二與書一封，飲之而神清。掘土而出，乃在空心巨樹之中，即為王所囚之島御苑也。王方欲自縊，忽見白影而罷。蝶引王至樹洞，得遇貞施。二人於燭案之前自為婚禮。既而王夢瓶破血流，懼；貞施解曰：『此非凶兆，乃紫袍加身之象也。』遂縱火焚室，由樹洞遁於海濱。

passages.text: The girl was stationed between the two candles, in front of the incense burners. The merchants knelt and began to pray. Cheng-Si consigned her soul to Heaven, and, without showing a trace of emotion, threw herself resolutely into the sea while the vessel continued on its way. Cheng-Si, who fully expected to drown in a few minutes, perceived with astonishment that she was resting on the surface of the water: in her plunge she had struck a gigantic sea turtle, which kept on swimming without seeming to be incommoded by his unusual burden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 6 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her mother appeared before her, borne on the fleecy sheets of a cloud: 'My daughter, be not afraid. Do not forsake the turtle who has saved your life until he has carried you safely to the shore.' The turtle, arriving close to the shore, turned aside into a deep subterranean passage and kept on swimming for several hours until it reached a point where the channel was very narrow; the innocent Cheng-Si jumped ashore, crying, 'Thank you, good turtle, for saving my life.' In the deep darkness she saw a ray of sunlight filtering through the rocky vault, and two small polished stone flasks, with a letter addressed to Cheng-Si herself: 'Drink the contents of these two bottles. One of them will wash away the fatigue of your long voyage; the other will clarify your ideas about the strange events which no doubt have troubled you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 6 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it so happened that the beautiful house and this fairy garden were the residence and place of recreation for the young King whom Ja-Jo-Mi, the unscrupulous, in his wickedness, had exiled. 'Why should I cling to life any longer? This everlasting loneliness, is it not the most cruel of punishments? Yes, it is better to die.' A rope tightly attached to the bough of a tree would be his instrument of deliverance; but the Prince hesitated: he had just seen a young girl, a beautiful vision in white, strolling along the shady paths of his garden. A single glimpse of a woman had this potent effect on him; he untied the cord from about his neck and started in headlong pursuit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 6 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Let's marry ourselves,' replied Cheng-Si, naively. They drew up a large table covered with a red cloth; two candles, signifying youth; a needle and thread, signifying union; and incense burners were placed on this improvised altar before which the betrothed pair knelt to pray to Heaven, after which they drank the sacramental wine from the same cup. One night the Prince dreamed of a large bottle the upper portion of which had been broken, whence a crimson stream was slowly flowing: 'Ja-Jo-Mi is going to kill me.' 'It does not have the meaning which you attribute to it,' rejoined Cheng-Si. 'When one breaks the neck of a bottle one holds it carefully by the bottom: the blood which trickles from the bottle signifies the royal purple with which you will be vested.' Placing burning brands in various parts of the house, they made their way through the hollow tree into the cave, and so to the seaside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 6 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: The Restoration of Ki-Si and the Fall of Ja-Jo-Mi

region.en: Chang-Yang inn to the Capital (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 昌陽至王城（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 7, eBook #78208

summary.en: A dream of San-Houni sends San-Syeng to the southern cape of the island of Cho-To, where he finds the King and his Queen on the beach disputing over who shall die. 'Give up your melancholy ideas. I will place my boat at your disposal and take you wherever you want to go.' The house on the island burns; the General reports the royal prisoner perished, and Ja-Jo-Mi, elated, orders a grand banquet. But at Chang-Yang the innkeeper tells San-Syeng that the garrisons and Mandarins are opposed to Ja-Jo-Mi, and if the King's son were not dead, the simplest thing would be to confer upon him the succession. Told the truth, the innkeeper prostrates himself, the Mandarin marches with troops to the inn, and the shout goes up through the length and breadth of the land — 'Hail, son, hail brother, hail to our King! Forward! If the wicked-hearted seek to restrain you, kill them. But look ever to the Sun; its warmth will give you strength and courage.' San-Syeng trains the army with bags of sand on their legs, takes the Capital in two days, and the populace bursting down the doors sweeps through the Prime Minister's palace like the demon waves of the Yellow Sea: Ja-Jo-Mi and his General are seized, and the King, ordering no one put to death, throws the guilty wretches into prison and reduces the taxes that oppress the people.
summary.zh: 山升夢亡父指路，至鳥島南端，遇夫婦爭死於海濱。乃以舟載之至昌陽。島中王居焚燬，將軍誤奏王死，子兆迷大喜設宴。而昌陽之驛丞、邑宰皆恨子兆迷。既知真王尚在，闔城迎於驛。王命山升為將，練兵負沙，兩日而抵王城。民眾破門而入，執子兆迷及其將軍下獄，宮亦火。王減稅安民，天下大悅。

passages.text: San-Houni appeared before him saying, 'You should take a boat and go to the southern cape of the island. There you will find the King and his Queen. But make haste, if you are too late you will find that the Prince has gone to abide with his ancestors.' He found on the beach a man and woman talking and gesticulating with great earnestness. 'We would like to cross the sea but having no boat and deprived of all resources, we are contemplating suicide. But I do not want my gentle companion to follow me to the grave, while she, on the other hand, is bent upon dying with me.' 'Give up your melancholy ideas. You are not going to die. I will place my boat at your disposal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 7 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'And suppose, for the sake of argument, that it were not true that the King's son were dead?' 'The simplest thing would be to confer upon him the succession to his father.' When he was alone with Ki-Si, San-Syeng asked: 'Would you like to join us in our fight against Ja-Jo-Mi?' At the question the Prince fell to the floor in a faint. Cheng-Si came running in terror to her husband, and San-Syeng cried to her, 'In Heaven's name, madame, tell me who you are!' 'My husband is Ja-Jo-Mi's victim, the King's son. I fell into the sea and was carried by a turtle to the island where the Prince was held captive. I became his wife and we fled from our prison together.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 7 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'O Beloved King! Night has vanished to give place to the day. Clouds were hiding the face of the Sun, and the flowers, deprived of light, were wasting away; but the wind has swept away the clouds and the light comes to us again. Hail, son, hail brother — hail to our King! Forward! If the wicked-hearted seek to restrain you, kill them. But look ever to the Sun; its warmth will give you strength and courage. We want you, beloved King! Now, away with tender things and soft things — we're off to war!' To toughen his men, San-Syeng made them attach small but heavy bags of sand to their legs for an entire day; the soldiers, now having only their weapons to carry, made rapid progress, and at the end of two days they were before the Capital City.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 7 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: The populace, having read the bamboo messages, arose in revolt: they were already advancing toward the Prime Minister's palace, burst down the doors and swept through the palace like the demon waves of the Yellow Sea. Ja-Jo-Mi and his General were seized, the palace set on fire, and simultaneously the King made a peaceful entry into the city at the head of his troops. 'No one shall be put to death. It will be sufficient, for the time being, to throw the guilty wretches into prison.' The new King ordered a reduction in the taxes which were oppressing his people, and sent out in all directions honest and devoted men to see that the decrees were observed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 7 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: The Feast of the Blind Men and the Opening Eyes

texts.period: Legend romance adapted by Charles M. Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile (1919)

source.work: Charles M. Taylor (adapt.), Winning Buddha's Smile: A Korean Legend (1919), ch. 9-10, eBook #78208

summary.en: Three years after the sacrifice, the Queen, sorrowing for her father, cries: 'Well, let's collect all the blind men in the Kingdom; invite them to a big feast. I'm going to give every one of them a little token.' Orders go to every Mandarin; at the feast Sun-Yen arrives tired and travel-stained, and when a lady of the Court grimaces at him he answers with the parable of the apple that looks attractive but contains a worm, and the flower swept by a gust from the tree that dies of a broken heart. Summoned to pass before the Queen one by one, the blind man tells his losses — 'I was powerful and I was exiled... my only consolation, a little daughter, was taken away. She furnished a beautiful example of filial love, sacrificing her life on the promise that I would regain my sight.' 'Don't you know Cheng-Si?' — 'My daughter,' stammers Sun-Yen, and instantly his eyes open and he sees before him the daughter he had thought forever lost; the prediction of the disciple is at last fulfilled. The King makes him Prime Minister, and when the King would avenge his father's defeat against Jin-Han, Sun-Yen asks instead a great meeting of the people: 'War is the worst of evils... Mankind, created to love and not to slaughter... Therefore, it is my opinion, sire, that we should not declare war. I do not wish the punishment of our guilty neighbors. Let us pardon them.' One day the Prime Minister disappears; possibly he had been carried to Heaven in a cloud, to his last and well-deserved home with his ancestors.
summary.zh: 王后集天下盲人赐宴。有老盲者至，容毀而言高妙，自述家難。后一聽而知為父，呼曰『貞施在此』。翁目忽明，父女相抱而泣。王遂拜翁為相。王欲伐鄰國以報父仇，翁於大宴之上集眾而問曰：『戰爭者，萬惡之源也。人生於世，以愛不以殺。願王罷兵，宥彼有罪之鄰。』眾皆歡呼稱善。一日，宰相忽不見——或乘雲而上，歸於其祖矣。

passages.text: 'Well, let's collect all the blind men in the Kingdom; invite them to a big feast. I'm going to give every one of them a little token.' No time was lost; orders were issued to every Mandarin to send every blind man in his jurisdiction to the Capital. When Sun-Yen arrived, tired and travel-stained, the servants led him to one of the ladies who could not conceal a grimace of disgust; but he answered: 'When you see an apple that looks attractive but contains a worm, you may contemplate its beauty but you keep your mouth away... I planted a beautiful fruit tree and it bore a single flower of exquisite beauty and charm. A gust of wind swept this flower toward the sea, and the latter, shorn of its only child, was slowly dying of a broken heart.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 9-10 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Because, my Queen, the world and religion and the government have caused me evils without number. I was powerful and I was exiled. I had the best of wives and I lost her. I became blind and my only consolation, a little daughter, was taken away. She furnished a beautiful example of filial love, sacrificing her life on the promise that I would regain my sight.' These words moved Cheng-Si profoundly, for in this sordid old man she recognized her father. She uttered a cry: 'Don't you know Cheng-Si?' 'My daughter,' stammered Sun-Yen, and instantly his eyes opened and he saw before him the daughter that he had thought forever lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 9-10 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Sire,' he said to the King, 'do you not believe that it would be advisable to know what your subjects think of this war before undertaking the campaign?... War is the worst of evils. It causes destruction beyond measure, and it is impossible to count the innocent ones who perish on the battlefield and at home... Mankind, created to love and not to slaughter... Therefore, it is my opinion, sire, that we should not declare war. I do not wish the punishment of our guilty neighbors although several of them have done me a great deal of harm. Let us pardon them.' These words met with unanimous approbation, and 'Twas a happy epoch for our country: content reigned everywhere.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 9-10 (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the Prime Minister disappeared. He could not be found. Possibly he had been carried to Heaven in a cloud — to his last and well-deserved home with his ancestors. For it has been proclaimed by The Great Teacher from the depths of his Wisdom, that all things having the appearance of Evil are transient and that Goodness will overcome and Virtue triumph: so, having passed through the ten stages of its life, our legend here cometh to an end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taylor, Winning Buddha's Smile, ch. 9-10 (1919); not verbatim.

title.en: Hamel and the Sparrow-hawk on the Shore of Quelpaert

texts.period: Shipwreck of 1653; narrative by Hendrik Hamel, retold in Louise Jordan Miln, Quaint Korea (1895)

source.work: Louise Jordan Miln, Quaint Korea (1895), ch. 1, eBook #56623

summary.en: In 1653 a Dutch boat was wrecked on the shore of Quelpaert: on the Sparrow-hawk was not only the governor-elect of Taiwan but also a sailor with a great gift for narrative writing, Hendrik Hamel, whose simple, straightforward record of thirteen years in Korea became Europe's most vivid photograph of the hermit kingdom. More than half the souls on board reached the shore; thirty-six were taken prisoners and held for thirteen years. 'On the 21st, a few days after the shipwreck, the commander made us understand by signs that he wished to see all we had saved from our wreck... it was sealed in our presence. While this was being done, some people were brought before him who had taken iron, hides, and other things that had drifted ashore from our boat; they were at once punished, and before our eyes, which showed us that the Korean officials did not mean us to be robbed of any of our goods. Each thief had thirty or more blows given him on the soles of his feet with a cudgel thick as a man's arm.' They were regarded by the populace as strangely interesting wild beasts; the King sent them an interpreter — Jan Wetteree, big, blue-eyed, red-bearded, captured from the Hollandra in 1627, who after twenty-seven years in Korea had forgotten his mother tongue but regained it in a month's intercourse with his countrymen; two of his mates died in 1635 fighting for Korea when she was invaded by the Manchus.
summary.zh: 1653年，荷蘭船麻雀鷹號破於濟州島，三十六人被留凡十三年。官吏封存其遺物，懲竊者以大杖擊足底三十。土人視之若異獸。王遣通事曰衛特里者——1627年因荷蘭船擱淺而被留之荷人，居韓二十七年而忘其鄉音，與同鄉相處月餘而復之。其同儕二人於1635年滿洲入侵時為韓戰死。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legend of first sustained European contact; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In 1653 a Dutch boat was wrecked on the shore of Quelpaert. To that shipwreck Europe owed her most vivid, if not her first photograph of Korea; for on the Sparrow-hawk was not only Min Heer Cornelius Lessen, the governor-elect of Tai-wan, but also a man of genius, a sailor who had a great gift for narrative writing — Hendrik Hamel. More than half the souls on board the Sparrow-hawk reached the shore of Korea. They were taken prisoners, and were held so for thirteen years and more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Miln, Quaint Korea, ch. 1 (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'On the 21st, a few days after the shipwreck,' writes Hamel, 'the commander made us understand by signs that he wished to see all we had saved from our wreck, and that we were to bring it from our tent and lay it before him. Then he gave orders that it should be sealed up, and it was so sealed in our presence. While this was being done, some people were brought before him who had taken iron, hides, and other things that had drifted ashore from our boat. They were at once punished, and before our eyes, which showed us that the Korean officials did not mean us to be robbed of any of our goods. Each thief had thirty or more blows given him on the soles of his feet with a cudgel thick as a man's arm and tall as a man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Miln, Quaint Korea, ch. 1 (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hamel and his fellows were enough of rarities to be regarded by the populace as strangely interesting wild beasts. The King of Korea was sending to them an interpreter, a man whose blood was their blood, whose tongue was their tongue: Jan Wetteree, a big, blue-eyed, red-bearded, robust Dutchman who had volunteered on board the Dutch ship Hollandra in 1626 and was caught with two mates when they went ashore for fresh water. Two of them died in 1635, fighting for the country of their enforced adoption when she was invaded by the Manchus; but Wetteree lived on, and twenty-seven years after his own capture was sent to interpret between his shipwrecked countrymen and their captors — his tongue had forgot its mother cunning, but the mother-tongue he regained in a month's intercourse with his countrymen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Miln, Quaint Korea, ch. 1 (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Profession Left Behind by Sin Nong

texts.period: Trade legend observed by Louise Jordan Miln, Quaint Korea (1895)

source.work: Louise Jordan Miln, Quaint Korea (1895), 'Some Curious Korean Customs', eBook #56623

summary.en: Painted upon suitable spots along the front of the Korean medicine shops runs the legend 'Sin Nong Yu Op' — the profession left behind by Sin Nong. This eminent person was a 'spiritual agriculturist,' the discoverer of both agriculture and medicine; and the pills sold in the shops to-day are supposed to be the counterparts of those invented by him. Worthily to render the legend, says Miln, we ought to translate it, 'Jones, successor to Aesculapius.'
summary.zh: 漢京藥肆門額皆題『神農遺業』四字。神農者，『神農』也，嘗百草、興農桑、創醫藥。今肆中所售丸散，皆云其方自神農所傳。米爾恩戲譯之曰：『瓊斯，醫神之後也。』

sensitivity.note: Trade-guild legend shared with Chinese Shen Nong heritage; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Painted upon suitable spots along the front of the building runs the legend, 'Sin Nong Yu Op,' — that is, 'the profession left behind by Sin Nong.' This eminent person was a 'spiritual agriculturist,' the discoverer of both agriculture and medicine; and the pills sold in the shops to-day are supposed to be the counterparts of those invented by him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Miln, Quaint Korea (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Worthily to render the legend, we ought to translate it, 'Jones, successor to Aesculapius.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Miln, Quaint Korea (1895); not verbatim.
